projects.title: AWS Portfolio & Serverless Contact
projects.intro: A public portfolio with private-origin delivery and an AWS contact integration.
projects.problem: A static website needs HTTPS delivery, controlled origin access and a contact channel without a dedicated application server.
projects.objective: Publish the portfolio through a custom-domain AWS delivery path and connect the browser contact form to an AWS endpoint.
projects.contribution: Built the static application and contact integration; documented private S3/CloudFront hosting and the Lambda/SES backend during Cloud and DevOps practical work.
projects.implementation: The browser sends bounded JSON contact requests to API Gateway. The documented hosting design uses a private S3 origin, CloudFront OAC, Route 53 and ACM. The GitHub workflow builds and validates the site, packages public assets and has a main-branch S3 deployment stage.
projects.decisions: Keep source templates and tests outside the public upload package. Serve content through the existing HTTPS distribution and use an API endpoint for contact requests rather than adding a web server.
projects.challenges: Resolved origin-access and CORS configuration issues in the documented project. The latest automated deployment was blocked by invalid stored AWS credentials; the current version was subsequently uploaded manually to S3 by the owner.
projects.verification: Reviewed application source, deployment workflow and packaging checks. Verified the production-origin CORS preflight. The owner confirmed the manual S3 upload worked. Lambda source, IAM policies, email delivery and current CloudFront configuration were not independently inspected.
projects.current: Public portfolio. Manual S3 upload confirmed by the owner; GitHub deployment credentials still require repair. No availability or email-delivery guarantee is claimed.
projects.lessons: An upload must include CSS, JavaScript, case studies and assets together. Validation and an explicit deployment package help prevent incomplete releases.
resume: Built private-origin S3/CloudFront portfolio hosting and integrated an API Gateway contact form with a documented Lambda/SES backend.
projects.label: 01 / CLOUD & DEVOPS

projects.title: Container delivery on AWS
projects.label: 02 / CLOUD & DEVOPS
projects.intro: A traceable path from a Git commit to a container registry.
projects.problem: A containerized web application needs a repeatable image build and a traceable release artifact.
projects.objective: Build a Docker image in CI, inspect it with Trivy and publish commit-tagged artifacts to Amazon ECR.
projects.contribution: Repository work includes a non-root Nginx Dockerfile and GitHub Actions build, scan and ECR publication workflow.
projects.implementation: The workflow builds on main/master pushes, tags images with the commit SHA and latest, runs Trivy, then pushes both tags to ECR. The Dockerfile switches to a non-root app user.
projects.decisions: Commit SHA tags connect an artifact to a source revision. The scan uses exit-code 0, so it reports findings without blocking publication. This is visibility, not an enforced security gate.
projects.challenges: The README describes Terraform and EKS resources that are absent from the reviewed source tree. The portfolio limits its claims to the Dockerfile and ECR pipeline that can be inspected.
projects.verification: Reviewed README.md, Dockerfile, .github/workflows/deploy.yml and the complete tree. No Terraform directory or Kubernetes manifest was present. The workflow was not executed and no AWS resources were inspected.
projects.current: Source implementation reviewed; current AWS deployment and build success are unverified. No uptime, failover, cost-saving or vulnerability-elimination result is claimed.
projects.lessons: Artifact publication and application deployment are separate stages. A future iteration can add enforced scan thresholds, pinned actions, OIDC credentials and a verified deployment stage.
resume: Built a GitHub Actions Docker build/Trivy-report/ECR-push pipeline with commit-SHA image tags and a non-root Nginx container.

projects.title: Kubernetes Application Orchestration
projects.intro: Declarative replicas, resource budgets and service discovery for a containerized web workload.
projects.problem: A single manually started container has no declarative replica count or stable service abstraction.
projects.objective: Practice Kubernetes workload management using a Deployment and a matching Service.
projects.contribution: Authored Kubernetes manifests for an Nginx deployment with three replicas, resource requests/limits and a NodePort service.
projects.implementation: deployment.yaml specifies three nginx:alpine replicas, CPU/memory requests and limits, and consistent app labels. service.yaml uses those labels to target port 80 and expose NodePort 30080.
projects.decisions: Separate workload and service definitions so pods can be replaced without changing the service contract. Declare resource requests and limits instead of leaving resource use implicit.
projects.challenges: Workload labels and service selectors must match for traffic to reach the pods. The manifests do not include HPA or readiness/liveness probes; those are next steps rather than implemented claims.
projects.verification: Reviewed deployment.yaml and service.yaml at revision 9ce9ef918c085f98d1cd99332271618b90933ed2, alongside the repository's lab documentation and screenshot inventory. No cluster was started or mutated in this portfolio task.
projects.current: Declarative Kubernetes lab. Three configured replicas are a manifest setting, not a claim of measured live capacity or availability.
projects.lessons: A useful orchestration example makes replicas, routing and resource budgets explicit. Probe behavior and failure recovery need their own reproducible tests.
resume: Defined a three-replica Nginx Deployment, CPU/memory requests and limits, and a label-selected NodePort Service in Kubernetes manifests.
projects.label: 03 / CLOUD & DEVOPS

projects.title: Dockerized Application on EC2
projects.intro: From a web application to a repeatable Linux container deployment.
projects.problem: A restaurant application needed a consistent build/start workflow and a workable host/container port arrangement.
projects.objective: Deploy the application to EC2, package it in Docker and automate the update sequence.
projects.contribution: Containerized the Velvet Restaurant application with Nginx, deployed it on EC2 Ubuntu and used a Bash deployment script to rebuild and restart the container.
projects.implementation: The README describes EC2 setup, Docker/Nginx configuration, restart policy and operational log/resource checks. Repository screenshots show a successful nginx:alpine image build and a completed deploy.sh execution on the EC2 host.
projects.decisions: Use a small static-web container and automate the build/stop/run sequence. Treat this as a single-host lab rather than claiming a rolling or zero-downtime release.
projects.challenges: A host Nginx process occupied port 80. The documented troubleshooting resolved the bind conflict; the deployment command also required the correct Docker build context.
projects.verification: Reviewed README.md and selected EC2 build/deployment screenshots at revision 8ae9704329ede935e824b318f522506dae95a820. The successful script run is historical evidence; the Dockerfile and deploy.sh are visible in screenshots but are not standalone tracked source files in this repository.
projects.current: Documented practical deployment. Current instance operation, HTTPS certificate state and uptime were not checked. No live IP is promoted as a current demo.
projects.lessons: Host services and container ports must be coordinated. Checking the build context, container logs and restart behavior gives a practical troubleshooting sequence.
resume: Containerized a restaurant site with Nginx on EC2 Ubuntu; automated rebuild/restart with Bash and resolved a host-port conflict.
projects.label: 04 / CLOUD & DEVOPS

projects.title: AWS Load Balancing & Auto Scaling
projects.intro: Exploring health-based routing and instance replacement on AWS.
projects.problem: A manually managed web server needs a traffic entry point and a repeatable replacement mechanism.
projects.objective: Practice ALB target groups, launch templates, Auto Scaling and network access controls.
projects.contribution: Configured a documented AWS web-tier lab using an ALB, EC2 launch template, Auto Scaling and target-group health checks.
projects.implementation: The repository describes the VPC, AMI/launch-template workflow, target group and scaling configuration. A reviewed console screenshot shows one registered target in Healthy state at capture time.
projects.decisions: Use the target group as the traffic/health boundary and a launch template to make instance replacement repeatable. The documented minimum capacity is one; that does not establish continuously redundant multi-AZ capacity.
projects.challenges: The README describes troubleshooting an unreachable endpoint through ALB security-group rules and exercising instance replacement. The reviewed screenshot does not establish a failover duration.
projects.verification: Reviewed README and target-group screenshots at revision 94f41812e27b4520f1890f93c4ae102c23662286. The tree contains documentation and images rather than infrastructure-as-code or the app.py mentioned in README.
projects.current: Historical lab evidence. No present endpoint, uptime percentage, scale-out capacity or zero-downtime result is claimed.
projects.lessons: Health checks, target registration and scaling settings should be verified separately. Infrastructure-as-code and a recorded replacement drill would make the lab easier to reproduce.
resume: Configured ALB target groups, EC2 launch templates and Auto Scaling in an AWS availability lab; documented security-group troubleshooting.
projects.label: 05 / CLOUD & DEVOPS

projects.title: AWS RDS Networking & Database Lab
projects.intro: Documenting a database tier with explicit network boundaries.
projects.problem: A database should be reachable by its application tier without broad public network access.
projects.objective: Practice RDS MySQL subnet placement, application-to-database connectivity and access rules.
projects.contribution: Documented an RDS MySQL lab covering private DB subnet groups, application-security-group ingress and connection checks.
projects.implementation: The README records creation of a DB subnet group, MySQL ingress restricted to an application security group, disabled public access and database connection verification. It also discusses Multi-AZ and managed credential storage.
projects.decisions: Express database access in terms of the application tier rather than open internet ingress. Keep conceptual discussion separate from demonstrated deployment results.
projects.challenges: Database connectivity depends on subnet placement and security-group rules. Current failover and restoration results require execution logs that are not supplied in the repository.
projects.verification: Reviewed README and the architecture asset inventory at revision f8566401b686ab69cf27b67c299c60e13fa0c2dc. No IaC, automated database tests or measured failure logs are present. The README's service descriptions and cost/performance statements were not adopted as verified claims.
projects.current: Documentation-backed lab. No measured recovery time, data-loss guarantee or current AWS deployment status is claimed.
projects.lessons: Subnet groups, connectivity tests and least-privilege ingress form useful practical evidence. A reproducible restore exercise would strengthen the project.
resume: Documented private RDS MySQL subnet groups, application-tier security-group ingress and database connectivity checks.
projects.label: 06 / CLOUD & DEVOPS

projects.title: CloudWatch Monitoring & Alerting Lab
projects.intro: Making infrastructure signals and alarm configuration visible.
projects.problem: An application can fail without a useful signal unless metrics, alarms and response procedures are designed together.
projects.objective: Practice metric selection, CloudWatch alarm setup and a documented notification path.
projects.contribution: Configured a CPU-utilization alarm and documented CloudWatch dashboard/SNS alerting practices for an AWS application lab.
projects.implementation: Reviewed console screenshots show a configured CPU alarm. The README describes dashboard widgets for compute, database and ALB signals, plus SNS notifications and cost-estimation exercises.
projects.decisions: Choose signals that connect compute load, application traffic and errors. Treat an alarm definition as configuration evidence rather than proof that an incident notification was delivered.
projects.challenges: The inspected alarm screenshot shows Insufficient data. A load/notification test and recorded state transition are still needed before claiming successful alert delivery or automatic remediation.
projects.verification: Reviewed README and alarm screenshots at revision fc216d35fd484dba7d1a16d49d95e709b92d5863. No current AWS access was used. Pricing-calculator estimates and percentage-savings claims were excluded from the portfolio/CV.
projects.current: Documented monitoring lab. Alarm configuration is evidenced; incident detection performance, notification delivery and savings are not measured here.
projects.lessons: Useful observability evidence includes a signal, threshold, state transition, notification receipt and response notes, not just a dashboard screenshot.
projects.evidence_level: README and reviewed alarm configuration screenshots
resume: Configured a CloudWatch CPU alarm and documented application metrics, dashboard design and an SNS notification path.
projects.label: 07 / CLOUD & DEVOPS

projects.title: Terraform foundations
projects.label: 08 / CLOUD & DEVOPS
projects.intro: Making a small piece of cloud infrastructure explicit and repeatable.
projects.problem: Manual cloud setup is difficult to inspect and reproduce from a source repository.
projects.objective: Practice the AWS provider and resource declaration in Terraform alongside a simple S3 delivery workflow.
projects.contribution: Repository work includes an AWS provider, an S3 bucket resource and a GitHub Actions S3 sync example.
projects.implementation: terraform/main.tf contains the AWS provider in us-east-1 and one S3 bucket resource. The separate workflow configures AWS credentials and runs aws s3 sync against a placeholder bucket.
projects.decisions: A small resource definition keeps the learning scope inspectable. The workflow is an example rather than a verified configured deployment because its destination is still a placeholder.
projects.challenges: README scope exceeds the checked-in infrastructure. Describe the actual S3 lab and make the configuration gap visible before anyone tries to reuse the workflow.
projects.verification: Reviewed terraform/main.tf, .github/workflows/deploy.yml, README.md and the tree. No Terraform apply, AWS calls or pipeline execution occurred.
projects.current: Foundational learning lab. No EKS provisioning, environment promotion or branch protection implementation is claimed.
projects.lessons: Infrastructure code is useful evidence only at the scope it actually implements. Next work includes provider pinning, state management and validation before deployment.
resume: Defined an AWS S3 bucket with Terraform and documented a GitHub Actions S3 sync example.

projects.title: NovaMart Multi-Agent RAG
projects.intro: AWS agent orchestration connecting policy retrieval with business-workflow tools.
projects.problem: A support workflow needs to combine policy knowledge with order/inventory actions while tracking the request across tools.
projects.objective: Explore specialized agents, retrieval-backed policy context, workflow state and observability on AWS.
projects.contribution: Developed Python multi-agent orchestration with Bedrock/Strands integrations, Knowledge Base retrieval helpers and DynamoDB/Lambda workflow tools.
projects.implementation: Authorized private-source review confirms orchestration, policy retrieval, workflow-state helpers, Guardrail application hooks, AgentCore deployment tooling and CloudWatch/X-Ray observability code. This public summary intentionally contains only high-level capabilities.
projects.decisions: Separate policy retrieval, workflow actions and response composition into specialized agent/tool responsibilities. Keep observability code alongside orchestration so requests can be traced across boundaries.
projects.challenges: Working integration code still needs runtime credentials, configured cloud resources and end-to-end tests. The presence of deployment tooling does not prove a current deployed AgentCore runtime.
projects.verification: Reviewed the owner-authorized private repository's current source structure and implementation symbols. No private source, configuration, resource identifiers or screenshots are republished. Cloud resources, model calls and tests were not executed.
projects.current: Private source implementation. A high-level walkthrough can be shared on request; no current cloud-runtime or benchmark result is claimed.
projects.lessons: A multi-agent project is stronger when retrieval, state transitions, tool authorization and request traces can be demonstrated independently.
resume: Built Python agent orchestration with Bedrock/Strands, policy retrieval and DynamoDB/Lambda workflow tools; added tracing and Guardrail hooks.
projects.label: 09 / AI ENGINEERING

projects.title: Digital Twin AI
projects.intro: From word embeddings to retrieval-grounded PDF conversations.
projects.problem: Finding useful information in text and PDFs requires retrieval of relevant context and a clear response when evidence is missing.
projects.objective: Combine embedding experiments, knowledge-base retrieval and document question answering in a Streamlit application.
projects.contribution: Implemented custom GloVe/search components, a retrieval pipeline with abstention behavior and Gemini-powered PDF chat with conversation context and source references.
projects.implementation: The knowledge-base path chunks text, retrieves similar passages and uses rule-based answer extraction. The PDF path extracts pages, ranks sentence embeddings and supplies selected context to Gemini. These are distinct paths; the knowledge-base demo is not described as generative LLM answering.
projects.decisions: Keep retrieval and answer generation separate. Preserve source/page information in the PDF path and return an insufficient-information result when the knowledge-base path cannot support an answer.
projects.challenges: Scanned PDFs need OCR beyond the current text extractor. Model availability and API quotas affect the PDF path. A retrieval-quality evaluation set is still a useful next step.
projects.verification: Reviewed pipeline.py, semantic_retriever.py, pdf_chat.py, three unit-test files and the CI workflow at revision 9a9acd80247d87d4bed53355209d14b2ff0a538f. A repository screenshot records 21 passing core tests; that is historical evidence, not a fresh test run in this task. No model request was made.
projects.current: Educational Streamlit demo supplied by the owner. Core code and historical test evidence reviewed; live model response quality and current hosted availability were not tested. Browser check on 31 October 2026 reached the Streamlit sleep page. The link is reachable; live model behavior was not tested.
projects.lessons: Embedding/search tests and explicit abstention are valuable, but they do not replace evaluation of the complete PDF/Gemini answering path.
projects.evidence_level: Source, tests and supplied demo evidence
resume: Built semantic retrieval and Gemini PDF chat with source references, custom embedding/search components and automated core-functionality tests.

projects.title: ETIKU AI
projects.intro: A conversational assistant with streaming responses and organized chat history.
projects.problem: A useful chat interface needs more than a model call: conversation management, response controls and understandable storage boundaries matter.
projects.objective: Build a branded assistant for learning, research and coding, with streaming output and manageable conversation history.
projects.contribution: Built the Streamlit chat interface, Gemini streaming integration, response-style/temperature controls and conversation create/search/rename/delete flows.
projects.implementation: assistant.py prepares chat history and streams Gemini output. The current entry point imports Supabase-backed authentication and conversation storage, while an older session-storage module remains in the tree. The supplied README/screenshots describe the earlier session-isolated public demo.
projects.decisions: Keep the model adapter, settings, authentication and storage in separate modules. Load API configuration through environment/Streamlit settings rather than placing credentials in client-facing code.
projects.challenges: The README still describes session-only storage while current code uses Supabase. Hosted behavior, database schema and row-level security need verification before claiming persistent multi-user isolation. RAG, PDF upload and voice remain roadmap items for ETIKU itself.
projects.verification: Reviewed assistant.py, etiku_app.py, session_storage.py and supabase_storage.py at revision 2310c6fea69f7284369494c4a7f849621fc6cd36. The owner supplied the Streamlit demo screenshot and URL. No sign-in, model request or database operation was performed.
projects.current: Streamlit demonstration with a newer authentication/storage implementation in source. No production-security or persistent-storage guarantee is made. Browser check on 31 October 2026 reached the Streamlit sleep page. The link is reachable; live model behavior was not tested.
projects.lessons: Storage behavior must match the README and UI copy. Clear module boundaries make the model, UI and storage layers easier to test independently.
resume: Built a Streamlit Gemini assistant with streaming responses, configurable response styles and conversation search, rename and delete controls.

projects.title: NASENI Research LIMS
projects.label: 12 / FULL-STACK
projects.intro: Connecting research records with traceable laboratory workflows.
projects.problem: Research projects, experiments and sample histories need a consistent record and clear access boundaries.
projects.objective: Explore a laboratory management workflow with authenticated access, sample tracking and audit records.
projects.contribution: Project work covers a React/TypeScript workspace and FastAPI API with role checks, sample tracking and audit logging.
projects.implementation: The API defines projects, experiments, samples and observations. JWT tokens expire after 30 minutes; role dependencies restrict writes and administration. Compose defines the database, backend and frontend services.
projects.decisions: Role checks run on API routes as well as in frontend navigation. Sample status changes and tracking events share a transaction, keeping the current state and history together.
projects.challenges: Sample updates can compete for the same record. The tracking route uses a database row lock and commits the status change, history event and audit entry together. Runtime concurrency behavior still needs testing.
projects.verification: Reviewed the repository tree, backend/app/main.py, backend/app/auth.py, frontend/package.json, frontend/src/app/App.tsx and compose.yaml. The README is stale: it says no frontend, while the source tree includes one. Application tests and deployment were not run in this portfolio task.
projects.current: Local development. No production deployment or institutional endorsement is claimed. This public summary uses only generic software architecture; no laboratory records, internal screenshots or institutional branding are reproduced.
projects.lessons: The code illustrates why authorization belongs on the server and why record history should be stored with the state change. A formal project retrospective is still to be supplied.
resume: Developing a React/TypeScript workspace and FastAPI API for research records and sample tracking.
Implemented JWT role checks and transactional sample-history and audit records in the reviewed source.

projects.title: RouteNG
projects.label: 13 / FULL-STACK
projects.intro: Exploring a more connected intercity travel experience in Nigeria.
projects.problem: Intercity carpooling needs coordinated ride listings, passenger requests and seat availability.
projects.objective: Build an MVP for Nigerian city search, ride management and driver/passenger booking workflows.
projects.contribution: Project source includes a vanilla HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend, Express API and PostgreSQL booking model.
projects.implementation: The API includes cookie-based JWT authentication, password hashing, city and ride search, vehicle management, seat-aware bookings, notifications and reviews. Paystack initialization and verification routes require server configuration.
projects.decisions: The booking route uses PostgreSQL transactions and SELECT FOR UPDATE to coordinate seat reservations. Express rate limits, Helmet and Zod validation provide baseline request controls.
projects.challenges: Booking state transitions and payment reconciliation need additional hardening. The README explicitly lists payment webhooks, identity verification and operational monitoring as pre-launch work. No real payments were tested.
projects.verification: Reviewed README.md, package.json, src/server.js and the repository tree. Frontend is vanilla JavaScript, not React. API routes are implemented in source; database, concurrency and end-to-end tests were not run here.
projects.current: MVP, not a verified live transportation service. Payment integration is optional and its production configuration is unverified. No paid booking or passenger-volume claim is made.
projects.lessons: The design highlights the importance of transactional seat allocation and explicit booking states. Payment verification and reconciliation need separate validation before launch.
resume: Built an HTML/JavaScript frontend and Express/PostgreSQL MVP for Nigerian ride search and booking workflows.
Added JWT cookie authentication and row-locked seat reservations; payments remain an optional integration.
